articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M Software Contract Renewed Without Bid Process
articles.dek: County commissioners quietly extended a decade-old records management deal last month. The vendor's lobbyist hosted three commissioners at a Destin fishing tournament in March.
brief: Escambia County commissioners approved a $2.3 million contract renewal with Civic Systems Solutions without competitive bidding on April 17
Three commissioners attended a March fishing tournament in Destin hosted by the company's registered lobbyist, Jeffrey Talbot
The original 2016 contract has been renewed three times; county procurement policy allows sole-source renewals under certain conditions
articles.body:
The consent agenda ran fourteen items long on April 17. Item nine took eleven seconds.

That was all the time Escambia County commissioners needed to approve a $2.3 million contract renewal with Civic Systems Solutions, a Tampa-based records management software company that has held the county's business since 2016. No discussion. No questions. No competing bids.

Six weeks earlier, three of those commissioners had spent a Saturday on a chartered fishing boat out of Destin Harbor. The host: Jeffrey Talbot, a Tallahassee lobbyist registered to represent Civic Systems Solutions before Escambia County government.

The Tournament

The Emerald Coast Invitational bills itself as a networking event for local officials and business leaders. Entry fees run $1,500 per boat. Talbot's firm, Capitol Strategies Group, sponsored two vessels this year.

Commission Chairman Doug Underwood, District 3 Commissioner Patricia Vance, and District 5 Commissioner Ray Mitchum all attended as Talbot's guests on March 8, according to a promotional video posted to the tournament's Facebook page. The video shows the three commissioners holding red snapper on the deck of a 42-foot Yellowfin center console.

Underwood confirmed his attendance when reached by phone. "It's a networking event. I network. That's part of the job," he said. Asked whether he saw any conflict with voting on Talbot's client's contract five weeks later, Underwood said: "I don't pick the consent agenda. Staff does."

Vance and Mitchum did not respond to requests for comment.

The Contract

Civic Systems Solutions provides the software Escambia County uses to manage public records requests, digitize archived documents, and track internal correspondence. The company's CivicVault platform handles an estimated 340,000 documents annually across 23 county departments.

The original contract, signed in October 2016, was worth $1.4 million over five years. It has been renewed three times since—in 2019, 2022, and now 2026. Each renewal increased the annual cost. The current deal runs $575,000 per year through 2029.

None of the renewals went through competitive bidding.

County Procurement Director Angela Stokes said the renewals comply with county policy. "When you have an existing system deeply integrated into operations, there's a provision for sole-source renewal," Stokes said in an email. "The switching costs and data migration risks can exceed any savings from competition."

The provision she referenced, Section 34.07(c) of the county procurement code, allows sole-source contracts when "the required service is available from only one source" or when "competitive solicitation would not serve the public interest." The April 17 agenda packet cited both justifications.

What the Records Show

Public records obtained by The Flightline show limited documentation of the county's decision to forgo bidding. A two-page memo from the Information Technology Department recommends renewal based on "operational continuity" and "satisfactory vendor performance." No performance metrics are attached. No cost comparison with alternative vendors appears in the file.

The memo is dated April 3—five days before the deadline for consent agenda items.

Talbot registered as a lobbyist with Escambia County in January 2024, according to the county clerk's lobbyist registry. His quarterly disclosure forms list Civic Systems Solutions as his only local client. The forms do not require disclosure of specific meetings or contacts with commissioners.

Florida's gift law prohibits lobbyists from giving gifts worth more than $100 to officials they lobby. A day of offshore charter fishing in Destin typically runs $2,500 to $4,000 for a private boat, though tournament packages vary. Whether the fishing trip constitutes a reportable gift depends on how the cost was structured.

The Florida Commission on Ethics would not comment on whether any complaint has been filed regarding the tournament. "We cannot confirm or deny the existence of any complaint," said commission spokesperson Dana Watkins.

A Pattern or an Oversight?

Escambia County renewed seven technology contracts without competitive bidding in fiscal year 2025, according to procurement records. Civic Systems Solutions is the largest by dollar amount.

Good-government advocates say the practice deserves more scrutiny, regardless of legal compliance.

"Sole-source renewals can be legitimate, but they can also become a way to avoid accountability," said Martha Kessler, policy director at Florida TaxWatch. "When the same vendor keeps getting renewed without competition, you have to ask whether taxpayers are getting the best deal."

Kessler said the fishing trip creates an additional concern. "Even if it's technically legal, it looks terrible. Perception matters in public contracting."

The next Escambia County Commission meeting is scheduled for May 21. Civic Systems Solutions representatives are not listed on the agenda.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The 17 Acres Behind Cordova Mall Nobody's Talking About
articles.dek: A Baton Rouge developer has assembled parcels along North Davis Highway for 18 months. Permit applications suggest a mixed-use project that would dwarf anything built in Pensacola since the pandemic.
brief: Pelican South Development LLC has quietly acquired seven contiguous parcels totaling 17.3 acres behind Cordova Mall since late 2024
Pre-application documents filed with Escambia County describe a 340-unit apartment complex with 45,000 square feet of ground-floor retail
The project would require rezoning from commercial to mixed-use and faces a planning board hearing in July with no public notice yet issued
articles.body:
The retention pond behind the Dillard's loading dock has been there so long that the egrets treat it like private property. They stand in the shallow water most mornings, unbothered by the delivery trucks or the employees smoking near the dumpsters. The pond sits on 2.4 acres that changed hands last October for $1.2 million.

Nobody announced the sale. No press release. The deed transferred from a Jacksonville-based holding company to an LLC registered in Baton Rouge four days before Christmas. It was the sixth parcel Pelican South Development LLC had acquired along the backside of North Davis Highway in 18 months.

The seventh came in February.

Combined, the seven parcels form a contiguous 17.3-acre rectangle stretching from the mall's northern service road to the tree line behind the Olive Garden. Property records show Pelican South paid a total of $8.7 million for land that Escambia County's property appraiser valued at $4.1 million before the acquisitions began.

The company has no website. Its registered agent is a law firm in Metairie, Louisiana. Phone calls to the firm go unanswered.

But documents do exist.

What the permits show

Pre-application materials filed with Escambia County's Development Services Department on March 14 describe a project called "Davis Commons." The 47-page submission requests a pre-application conference to discuss a mixed-use development featuring 340 apartment units across four five-story buildings, 45,000 square feet of ground-floor retail and restaurant space, and a 650-space parking structure.

The documents list an estimated construction cost of $127 million.

For context: The entire West Main development downtown—the largest mixed-use project completed in Pensacola since the pandemic—cost $54 million and contains 180 units.

Davis Commons would be more than twice that size.

The pre-application materials were prepared by Goodwin Engineering, a civil engineering firm based in Mobile with offices in Pensacola. Reached by phone last week, a Goodwin project manager confirmed the firm had prepared the documents but declined to discuss the project or identify the developer.

"We're not authorized to speak on behalf of the client," he said.

The pre-application conference—a routine procedural step where developers meet with county staff to discuss requirements before filing formal applications—was held April 2. Records of what was discussed are not public until a formal application is submitted.

The zoning problem

All seven parcels are currently zoned C-2, Escambia County's general commercial designation. C-2 allows retail, restaurants, offices and hotels. It does not allow residential.

Building 340 apartments requires rezoning to MU-S, the county's suburban mixed-use category. That means a public hearing before the Planning Board, followed by another hearing before the Board of County Commissioners. Both require public notice: signs posted on the property, letters mailed to nearby property owners, legal advertisements in the Pensacola News Journal.

None of that has happened yet.

According to the county's development calendar, the next available Planning Board hearing for a rezoning application filed in May would be July 17. Applications must be submitted 45 days before a hearing. That deadline is June 2.

If Pelican South files by June 2, the first public notice would go out around June 17. Residents of the Cordova Park and Carriage Hills neighborhoods—the established single-family subdivisions that border the project site to the east and north—would receive mailed notices around the same time.

As of Friday, no rezoning application had been filed.

Who is Pelican South?

Louisiana Secretary of State records show Pelican South Development LLC was formed in April 2024. Its registered agent is Lemoine & Associates, a law firm in Metairie that specializes in real estate transactions. The firm's website lists no attorneys by name.

The LLC's manager is listed as "PSH Ventures LLC," another Louisiana entity formed the same week. PSH Ventures' manager is listed as "Heron Capital Partners LLC," formed in 2019.

Heron Capital Partners has an address on Corporate Boulevard in Baton Rouge. The building houses several commercial real estate firms, including one called Acadiana Development Group.

Acadiana Development Group's website describes the company as a "vertically integrated multifamily developer" with projects in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama. The site lists no projects in Florida.

Calls to Acadiana Development Group were not returned. An email sent to the company's general inquiry address received an automated reply stating the office was closed for a "company retreat" through May 15.

Whether Acadiana Development Group is the actual developer behind Pelican South remains unconfirmed. The corporate structure—three layers of LLCs between the land-owning entity and any identifiable principals—is common in commercial real estate but makes direct attribution difficult without cooperation from the parties involved.

What the neighbors don't know

Karen Whitfield has lived on Doris Drive, in Carriage Hills, for 31 years. Her back fence sits roughly 200 feet from the northern boundary of the project site.

She had never heard of Pelican South Development or Davis Commons until a reporter showed her the pre-application documents last Tuesday.

"Five-story buildings?" she said, reading from the site plan. "Where exactly?"

The site plan shows the two northernmost apartment buildings positioned along the tree line, separated from the Carriage Hills fence line by a 30-foot landscaped buffer. The buildings would stand approximately 58 feet tall at the roofline—visible from Whitfield's backyard even with mature trees in between.

"Nobody's told us anything," she said. "Not the county. Not anybody."

Technically, nobody is required to. Florida's land development regulations require public notice only after a formal application is filed. Pre-application conferences are confidential. Land acquisitions are public record, but monitoring them requires knowing where to look and what to look for.

The Carriage Hills Homeowners Association holds monthly meetings at Cordova Park Elementary. The next meeting is May 21. The agenda, posted on the HOA's website, includes "landscaping committee update" and "pool rules reminder." It does not mention the development.

HOA president Jim Decker said he was unaware of the project. Told about it by phone, he paused for several seconds.

"We're going to need to have a conversation," he said.

The traffic question

North Davis Highway between Cordova Mall and Airport Boulevard already operates at or above capacity during peak hours. Florida Department of Transportation traffic counts from 2024 show the segment carrying 47,000 vehicles per day—roughly 10 percent above the road's designed capacity.

Adding 340 apartment units and 45,000 square feet of retail would generate an estimated 3,200 additional vehicle trips per day, according to standard ITE trip generation rates. The pre-application materials acknowledge this and indicate that a formal traffic impact study will be required.

But traffic studies in Escambia County are prepared by the developer's engineers and reviewed by county staff. The county does not conduct independent traffic analysis for private development projects.

The pre-application materials propose two access points: one on North Davis Highway and one connecting to the mall's existing service road network. No access is proposed through the Carriage Hills neighborhood.

Whether that configuration is sufficient—or whether the county will require additional improvements to North Davis Highway as a condition of approval—will not be known until formal review begins.

What happens next

If Pelican South files a rezoning application by June 2, the project enters the public review process. The Planning Board hearing would likely occur July 17. The Board of County Commissioners could vote as early as August.

If approved, construction could begin in early 2027.

If the company does not file by June 2, the timeline pushes back by at least a month. The September Planning Board meeting is already full, according to county staff, which would delay the first hearing to October at the earliest.

Nothing in the pre-application materials indicates urgency. But the pace of land acquisition—seven parcels in 18 months, all paid above appraised value—suggests a developer operating on a schedule.

The egrets will keep fishing in the retention pond until someone tells them otherwise. That could be sooner than anyone in Carriage Hills expected.

articles.label: Local Economy
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings $31M to Pensacola. Most Businesses on Palafox Won't See It.
articles.dek: Hotel chains near the base and national restaurant franchises capture the bulk of airshow spending. Downtown merchants say the math hasn't worked in years.
brief: Visit Pensacola estimates Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show generated $31.2 million in economic impact, but spending concentrates near NAS Pensacola and along the airport corridor
Downtown Pensacola businesses report flat or declining sales during airshow weekend despite record attendance of 185,000 spectators
Hotel occupancy data shows properties within three miles of the base averaged 97% capacity while downtown hotels saw typical May weekend numbers
articles.body:
At 11:47 a.m. on Saturday, six F/A-18 Super Hornets screamed over Pensacola Bay in diamond formation. The sound hit downtown three seconds later—a physical pressure against the chest, the windows of Palafox Street boutiques vibrating in their frames.

Inside Southern Salvage Antiques, owner Diane Kelley watched two customers look up from a mahogany dresser, startled. They didn't buy anything. By 2 p.m., when the show ended, she'd made four sales totaling $127.

"I used to close the shop and go watch," Kelley said. "Now I stay open because I keep thinking this will be the year it changes. It never does."

The 2026 Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show drew an estimated 185,000 spectators over two days—a record, according to Naval Air Station Pensacola officials. Visit Pensacola, the area's tourism marketing organization, projects $31.2 million in total economic impact. That figure includes hotel stays, restaurant meals, gas purchases, and retail spending.

The question downtown merchants keep asking: Where does that money actually land?

Following the Dollars

The Flightline reviewed hotel occupancy data from STR, a hospitality analytics firm, and spending patterns from Square merchant reports shared by seven downtown business owners. The picture that emerges shows two separate economies operating during airshow weekend.

Hotels within a three-mile radius of NAS Pensacola—properties along Navy Boulevard, near the airport, and in the Cordova Mall corridor—averaged 97.3% occupancy Friday and Saturday nights. Average daily rates hit $189, up from $141 during a typical May weekend.

The Hilton Garden Inn on Airport Boulevard sold out by Tuesday of airshow week. The Hampton Inn on Navy Boulevard stopped taking reservations the Monday before.

Downtown, the numbers look different. The Pensacola Grand Hotel reported 84% occupancy—solid, but within normal range for a pleasant May weekend. The Sole Inn & Suites on Palafox saw 79%.

"Our guests this weekend were here for a wedding," said Marcus Chen, front desk manager at the Sole. "Maybe three rooms mentioned the airshow. People watching the Blues aren't staying downtown. They're staying where they can get to the base."

The Geometry of Spectacle

The math is simple. NAS Pensacola sits at the southern tip of the city, past the industrial port, beyond the reach of a casual walk. Spectators enter through Barrancas Gate, watch from bleachers erected on the flight line, and leave through the same gate. The route funnels traffic north on Navy Boulevard, then west toward I-110 or east toward the beach.

Downtown Pensacola sits three miles northeast. It requires an intentional detour.

"You're asking 185,000 people, most of whom drove from Mobile or Destin or somewhere in Alabama, to add an extra stop after sitting in the sun for four hours," said Tom Garner, who owns a men's clothing store on Palafox. "They want air conditioning and the fastest route to their hotel."

Garner's Saturday sales: $340. His average Saturday in May: $890.

The restaurants capturing airshow traffic aren't downtown either. They're the chains along Airport Boulevard—Chili's, Olive Garden, Longhorn Steakhouse—and the fast-casual spots near the base. A manager at the Chili's on Airport Boulevard, who asked not to be named because she wasn't authorized to speak publicly, said Saturday's sales were "easily double" a normal weekend.

"We called in extra staff. We had a wait from 5 p.m. until close," she said.

A Persistent Hope

Visit Pensacola has tried to bridge the gap. This year's Homecoming marketing included a "Blue Angels Weekend Downtown" campaign, with shuttle service from Palafox to the show grounds. The shuttle ran Friday and Saturday, departing from the Saenger Theatre parking lot.

Ridership data wasn't available by press time. Anecdotally, downtown business owners reported seeing the shuttle circulate mostly empty.

"The intention is good," said Rachel Morrison, owner of Bodacious Bookshop on Palafox. "But people don't come downtown to catch a shuttle. And after the show, they don't want to ride a bus back to where their car isn't."

Morrison kept her shop open late Saturday, until 8 p.m., hoping to catch families wandering downtown for dinner. She made one sale after 5 p.m.—a $14 children's book about airplanes.

The disconnect isn't new. Downtown merchants have raised the issue at Pensacola City Council meetings and Downtown Improvement Board sessions for at least a decade. Proposals have included extended trolley service, coordinated restaurant specials, and a Friday evening "Blue Angels Block Party" on Palafox.

None have moved forward. The reasons vary—cost, logistics, competing interests—but the underlying challenge remains. The airshow happens at the base. The base isn't downtown.

The Beneficiaries

For businesses positioned along the airshow corridor, Homecoming Weekend delivers.

Joe Patti's Seafood, located a mile from NAS Pensacola, extended hours and brought in extra staff. Owner Frank Patti III said Friday and Saturday sales combined exceeded $80,000—roughly triple a typical weekend.

"We've been doing this 30 years," Patti said. "You plan for it like a hurricane, except nobody boards up the windows."

Gas stations along Navy Boulevard reported lines throughout the weekend. The Circle K at the corner of Navy and Fairfield sold out of premium unleaded by 1 p.m. Saturday.

The pattern repeats in Escambia County's tourism tax collections. May typically shows a modest bump from the airshow, but the dollars flow to hospitality—hotels and restaurants—not retail. The county's 4% tourist development tax, which funds beach renourishment and tourism marketing, draws from hotel stays, not antique shop purchases.

What Would Change It?

Garner, the Palafox clothier, has thought about this for years. His answer: nothing realistic.

"You'd have to move the show," he said. "Put it over the bay, let people watch from downtown. But then you lose the base, you lose the history, you lose the whole point."

The Blue Angels have performed at NAS Pensacola since 1946. The base is their home. The Homecoming show exists because the team returns there.

Other cities have experimented with waterfront airshows. Chicago's Air and Water Show unfolds over Lake Michigan, viewable from miles of shoreline. Cleveland's show happens over Lake Erie, visible from downtown. Both generate significant foot traffic in adjacent commercial districts.

Pensacola's geography works against that model. The deepwater port occupies the downtown waterfront. Commercial flight paths restrict airshow maneuvers over the bay. The base offers the only practical venue.

So downtown merchants watch the jets trace contrails overhead, feel the windows shake, and wait for customers who mostly don't come.

"It's a beautiful show," Kelley said, locking her shop at 5:30 Saturday. She'd been open nine hours. Total sales: $214. "I just wish it was beautiful for business too."
